extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and media professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and routines that shape how news is gathered, selected, framed, and produced across media organizations; emphasizes source relations, organizational constraints, medium differences, and strategic manipulations of news routines. Useful for evaluating or designing journalistic practice and news output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoop / Exclusives as standard of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting first what everyone else will want is the standard in the highly ambiguous process of deciding what news is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusives provide a measurable performance standard (a clockable race) and organizational evaluation metric; they help claim special excellence but are exceptional rather than the norm. Risk: reporters should avoid getting too far ahead of the pack and being wrong in full view of the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack coverage / synchronization
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mainstream media all go after the same stories, organizations are synchronized and coverage becomes 'pack coverage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack mentality reduces uniqueness; desire to be unique is outweighed by risk of being different and wrong. This constrains novelty in story selection and makes many outlets cover the same events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific organizational differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media must create different structures to carry out their functions (technology, economic support, frequency, political relationship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print and broadcast differ in routines because of staff size, technology, publishing frequency, and regulatory context; these organizational differences produce different reporting behaviors and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television reporters' source dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because television news stations typically have smaller staffs and daily story demands, television reporters are often subservient to their sources and dependent on public relations control efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller staffs and technological constraints make TV reporters more reliant on routine source-provided material; this dependency shapes story selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television 'standups' affect attribution and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Television news stories have traditionally relied on reporter 'standups' which favor snappy language and often fail to provide the usual attribution for assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standups are often recorded before final story compilation, so last-minute changes can leave claims with inadequate support. This practice increases risk of under-attributed or weakly supported on-camera claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-type reliance differences (broadcast vs print)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast reporters rely more on routine activities (news conferences, visually dramatic events); print reporters rely more on personal sources (experts, legislative leaders) which yield background information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different source reliance produces different kinds of stories—broadcast favors visual drama, print favors depth and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational commitment affects reporter status and beat access
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of an organization's commitment to a steady presence (e.g., at a statehouse) prevents reporters from 'paying their dues' and reaching the 'inner club.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter rank in the journalists' own hierarchy and access to sources depend on organizational staffing commitments and presence; this affects ability to cultivate sources and obtain insider information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and production constraints (TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast reporters report having fewer layers of editorial oversight; it's harder to change a reporter's video package than to edit newspaper copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the presentational aspects of television require integrating reporter work into a larger production, once filed the reporter relinquishes control; production constraints influence content, pacing, and what can be altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency on external suppliers (sources) for raw material
rubrics_metrics.description: The media rely on external suppliers of raw material—speeches, interviews, corporate reports, government hearings—which have a major influence on media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppliers (sources) dictate routines; sometimes media and sources adapt mutually, making it hard to determine which shaped the routines. Reliance on suppliers structures what is available to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lawsuits and legal processes as routine story sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reports often rely on lawsuits in progress; many potential sources can't comment due to litigation, and plaintiff-side sources with clear points of view are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawsuit-based coverage provides conveniently available, articulate sources but may present a distorted view because of one-sided access and the adversarial format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press conferences and photo opportunities as source routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Photo opportunities and press conferences are routines employed by sources to get into the news; they are choreographed and allow sources to regulate release of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press events can be orchestrated: planted questions, ignored hostile reporters, and evasive responses; such routines let sources set the terms and reduce reporters' ability to control framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release reliance and verbatim use
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of the press release and press conference reduced the ability of reporters to get scoops; press releases are sometimes used verbatim (nearly 20 percent in one study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially resource-poor outlets rely more on ready-made press material. Reliance on press releases makes journalists more manipulable and reduces original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of information channels (routine, informal, enterprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sigal's definitions: routine channels (official proceedings, press releases, press conferences, nonspontaneous events); informal channels (background briefings, leaks, nongovernmental proceedings, reports from other news orgs); enterprise channels (reporter-initiated interviews, spontaneous events, independent research, reporters' own analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings show heavy use of routine channels (e.g., 58% of page-one stories), with enterprise channels much less used; primary-channel leads are overwhelmingly routine, indicating institutional preference for routinized sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on routine channels reduces enterprise reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the channels used in leading stories, routine channels dominate (e.g., 72% of primary channels), while enterprise is a small fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy routine-channel use reflects both official efforts to confine dissemination to routine channels and reporters' reliance on them; this reduces investigative and independent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official sources institutionalize information control
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization of governmental power enhanced ability to control information, and official sources institutionalized routines (press conferences, press releases, briefings) to regulate release of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official routines let sources set rules for dissemination, often making information release efficient and controllable while giving the appearance of openness; this institutionalization draws scholarly attention because it's visible and impactful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background briefings and unattributable information norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefings can be 'off the record,' 'deep background,' or 'background'—rules that limit attribution: off-the-record cannot be used, deep background can be used but not quoted or attributed, background can be attributed vaguely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While objectivity routines normally dictate naming sources, reporters accept these ground rules to obtain information; this compromises accountability and attribution norms when reporters prioritize access over named sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaks as a routine tactic with multiple functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaks are generally initiated by officials as a tactic in intraorganizational infighting and serve functions such as floating trial balloons, blowing the whistle, promoting or sabotaging policy, currying favor, or enhancing the leaker's ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaks are less common than other channels but more routine than exceptional; they are often targeted at single reporters (exclusives) and have strategic purposes for insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and professionalization drive source reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters rely on official sources because government provides a convenient, regular flow of authoritative information which is more efficient than labor-intensive research; professionalization strengthens press–state connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bargain: reporters trade the hard way (legwork) for the easy way (inside tips), accepting routine-channel news as a cost of obtaining occasional exclusives; professional norms of objectivity make officials useful validators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access-influence bargain: reporters transmit source-preferred frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are willing, in exchange for 'access,' to transmit the images their sources wish transmitted and to present source-provided reconstructions as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covering campaigns and other access-driven beats often leads journalists to present staged or set-up events as spontaneous news; reporters accept source frames to secure access and career-related rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sourcing homogeneity shapes analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrow, homogenous, elite group of experts dominates political discourse; they are often conservative, linked to think tanks and prestigious institutions, and provide succinct, predictable responses that reinforce conventional wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers favor experts whose centrist/predictable views 'reinforce their own understanding' and create an 'illusion of objective reporting'; repeated use of the same experts reduces diversity of perspectives and critical challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of routines by sources (scripted spontaneity, visual press releases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources manipulate routines through techniques such as scripted spontaneity, visual press releases, restricting unscripted encounters, beaming unedited appearances, and letting organizations tap into computer-compiled releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tactics aim to minimize press editing and shape news visually and textually before journalists can interpret it; they represent an attempt by sources to become de facto producers of news content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to source bureaucracy and beat construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' beat routines are constructed around the structure of the bureaucracies they cover; reporters make 'rounds' of institutional centers (courts, sheriff, police) in scheduled sequences to maximize efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bureaucratic organization routinizes newswork, directing attention to institutional points yielding concentrated information and rendering many occurrences 'nonevents' because they do not fit the bureaucratic perspective or scheduled purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted access, pool systems, and compliance in wartime reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Pool systems and military-imposed restrictions limit journalists' access, obliging secrecy and close control; reporters adapt by accepting restrictive routines and may become more compliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricted access conditions (e.g., Gulf War) led reporters to accept military frames, be monitored by handlers, and have stories reviewed by public information specialists; noncompliance risks future access and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-optation signaled by language and symbolic alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-optation of journalists by sources can be signified in news discourse by use of we/our (e.g., 'we invaded,' 'our troops'), binding reporters rhetorically to governmental and military interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such rhetorical inclusion indicates absorption of source frames into reporting norms and reflects an interpretive framework that works against alternative perspectives and critical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbiotic routines produce mutual benefits and shape content
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines can become mutually advantageous—media get dramatic footage cheaply, the military/officials get favorable framing, and defense manufacturers get advertising—creating a symbiotic relationship that shapes news content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying these interlocking routines explains why certain forms of content (high-tech visuals, dramatic footage) are popular: they serve the practical interests of multiple parties and reinforce selected framings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines as constraints shaped by multiple pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines form the immediate environment for media workers; they both constrain individuals and are themselves functions of constraints such as audience attention, organizational resources, and source-provided material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The event focus and other routines are functional for organizations and audiences but also provide levers for powerful external actors to influence content; less advantaged sources must conform to these routines to gain coverage.
